items.value: The challenge is to achieve hard work, brotherhood and national unity
items.reasoning: Each element of option D is anchored in the passage: 'We have hard work ahead' opens it; 'All of us, to whatever religion we may belong, are equally the children of India' is brotherhood; and 'We cannot encourage communalism or narrow-mindedness, for no nation can be great whose people are narrow' is national unity. Option A misreads 'live up to that high standard', which is a standard of conduct, as a standard of living, and the passage never speaks of material progress. The runner-up is B: 'equal privileges' and 'fulfilment of destiny' are both verbatim in the passage, so B would win if the examiner read the anti-communalism sentence as being about 'political tolerance'. It is rejected because the communalism the passage names is religious, not political, and 'brotherhood' plus 'national unity' capture that sentence far more directly. Option C fails outright: the passage says nothing about a spirit of adventure or economic parity.

items.value: The General Will is the collective good, distinct from the private wills of individuals
items.reasoning: The passage has the individual place his person and power 'in common under the supreme direction of the General Will', and speaks of a 'corporate capacity' in which each member is 'an indivisible part of the whole'. That language makes the General Will something belonging to the collective body, not to the individuals severally. Option A is the trap: it describes Rousseau's 'will of all', the mere sum of private wills, which he expressly distinguishes from the General Will. B confuses the General Will with representation, which Rousseau rejected. D narrows it to material interests, a restriction the passage nowhere makes.

items.value: In a mature democracy force is reduced to a marginal phenomenon in the actual exercise of sovereignty
items.reasoning: The passage says that where political maturity is high, conflict between the sovereign law-making body and the organized will of the people 'seldom occurs'. Force is what a sovereign resorts to when its will meets resistance, so if conflict is rare, force is rare too - marginal, which is exactly what D says. A and B assert the opposite, that force is the main phenomenon. C overstates in the other direction: 'seldom' means infrequent, not never, so calling force 'irrelevant' claims more than the sentence supports.

items.value: The passage is about the duty to vote
items.reasoning: The decisive phrase is 'it is to refuse one's political responsibility while enjoying the benefits of a free political society'. A responsibility that one can refuse and be blamed for refusing is a duty, not a right or a freedom. B and C both frame voting as an entitlement, whereas the passage is reproaching those who decline to exercise it. D is too broad: the passage names political participation only to establish that voting is 'an essential part' of it, and the reproach is aimed specifically at not voting.

items.value: Despair or an unhappy national condition sometimes brings a dictator to power
items.reasoning: The last sentence states that a dictator 'often reaches his position of power through chance, very often through the unhappy state of his country' - that is precisely 'despair in a country sometimes leads to dictatorship'. A misreads the passage: it says it is possible for others to foresee that a man will become a leader because 'one can see his qualities of character', not that the leader foresees his own rise. B inserts an 'only' the passage never uses. C is prescriptive advice the passage does not give; it is describing how dictators arise, not what leaders ought to do.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - the creative use of leisure by a minority has been the chief source of human progress
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 restates the passage's closing sentence almost exactly: 'the creative use of leisure by a minority in societies has been the mainspring of all human progress beyond the primitive level' - creative use maps to producing new and original things, a minority to some people, and mainspring to chief source. Assumption 1 fails twice over. The passage says the gift of leisure 'may be abused by people who have had no experience of making use of it', which contradicts the claim that people 'always' value it; and it opens by denying that accumulating material possessions is the great blessing, so it certainly does not assume people spend leisure acquiring them.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - studying history is essential for those who aspire to leadership
items.reasoning: The passage endorses the view that 'a working knowledge of ancient history is necessary to the intelligent interpretation of current events' and then commends studying famous battles 'for the lessons they contain for those of us who lead or aspire to leadership', which supports assumption 2. Assumption 1 shifts the subject: what the study is said to reveal is 'qualities and attributes which enabled the winners to win' and the deficiencies that made losers lose - lessons about leadership, not about the conduct or technology of modern warfare, a term the passage never uses. The runner-up is C. It would win if 'the same pattern recurs consistently, again and again, throughout the centuries' is read as carrying the lessons forward into present-day war, making assumption 1 valid too; the sentence is about a recurring pattern of leadership qualities, which is why that reading is set aside here. D would win only if 'essential' is judged a stronger claim than the passage's 'benefits', but the passage's own word 'necessary' makes that unlikely.

items.value: The 5th person weighs 50 kg
items.reasoning: Total weight of all 9 persons is 9 x 50 = 450 kg. The first five weigh 5 x 45 = 225 kg and the last five weigh 5 x 55 = 275 kg. Those two groups are persons 1-5 and persons 5-9, so together they cover all nine persons and count the 5th person twice: 225 + 275 = 500 kg. The excess over the true total is the double-counted person, so the 5th person weighs 500 - 450 = 50 kg.

items.value: Nirmala is both a tennis player and a bank employee
items.reasoning: There are three bank employees, and Vimala and Kamla are two of them. Among Amala, Kamla, Komala and Nirmala - the four Sociology postgraduates - exactly two are bank employees; Amala and Komala are stated to be unemployed, so those two must be Kamla and Nirmala. The three bank employees are therefore Vimala, Kamla and Nirmala. Nirmala is also named as one of the tennis players, so she satisfies both conditions. Amala and Komala are unemployed and so cannot qualify, and Shyamala is not among the three bank employees.

items.value: Neither P > Q nor Q > P can be concluded; the comparison depends on how much larger A is than B
items.reasoning: P - Q = (0.40 - 0.50)A + (0.65 - 0.50)B = 0.15B - 0.10A, which is zero exactly when A = 1.5B. Since the only condition given is A > B, both sides of that threshold are reachable. Take A = 1.1 and B = 1: P - Q = 0.15 - 0.11 = 0.04, so P > Q. Take A = 2 and B = 1: P - Q = 0.15 - 0.20 = -0.05, so Q > P. Two admissible sets of values give opposite results, so no fixed relation holds and D is correct.

items.value: None of 30, 90 or 120 days is correct; on a 24-hour clock the watches agree again only after 360 days
items.reasoning: One watch loses 2 minutes a day and the other gains 2 minutes a day, so the gap between them widens by 4 minutes every 24 hours. On a 24-hour clock the two faces show the same reading again only when that gap reaches a whole 24 hours, that is 1440 minutes, which takes 1440 / 4 = 360 days. After 30 days the gap is only 120 minutes, after 90 days it is 360 minutes and after 120 days it is 480 minutes - 2, 6 and 8 hours respectively, none of them a full day. So all three offered periods fail and D is correct.

items.value: 240 households earn between Rs 1,00,000 and Rs 2,00,000 per year
items.reasoning: Households earning between Rs 30,000 and Rs 1,00,000 are those left after removing the 12 per cent earning below Rs 30,000 and the 22 per cent earning above Rs 1,00,000, which is 100 - 12 - 22 = 66 per cent. Since that band holds 990 households, the total is 990 / 0.66 = 1500 households. The band from Rs 1,00,000 to Rs 2,00,000 is the 22 per cent above one lakh less the 6 per cent above two lakh, that is 16 per cent, and 16 per cent of 1500 is 240.

items.value: 24 seconds, taking the striking time as directly proportional to the number of strikes
items.reasoning: Treating the time as proportional to the number of strikes, each strike accounts for 12 / 5 = 2.4 seconds, so ten strikes take 24 seconds. Note that the usual convention for this puzzle - that five strikes span four intervals, giving 3 seconds per interval and 9 x 3 = 27 seconds for ten strikes - produces an answer that is not among the options, so the item as printed cannot be intended that way. Writing t for the duration of one strike and g for one gap, 5t + 4g = 12 forces the answer for ten strikes, 10t + 9g, to lie between 24 (when g = 0) and 27 (when t = 0); 24 is the only option inside that range, which is the strongest evidence for it. The runner-up is D, 30 seconds, which arises from the inconsistent hybrid of computing 3 seconds per interval from four intervals and then multiplying by ten rather than nine; it would win only if the examiner made that specific slip.

items.value: Neither conclusion follows from the statement
items.reasoning: The statement asserts only that morning walk is beneficial for health. Conclusion 1 reverses and universalises this: knowing that a morning walk helps tells us nothing about what all healthy people actually do, since health can be maintained in other ways. Conclusion 2 upgrades 'good for' into 'essential for', which is a claim of necessity the statement never makes - something can be beneficial without being indispensable. Neither is a valid inference.

items.value: The mean of all thirteen numbers is 47
items.reasoning: For five consecutive odd numbers the mean is the middle one, so if the mean of the first five is 39 the third number is 39 and the first is 39 - 4 = 35. The thirteen numbers are therefore 35, 37, ..., 59, all of which are two-digit as required. For thirteen consecutive odd numbers the mean is again the middle term, the seventh, which is 35 + 2 x 6 = 47.

items.value: D and E together hold 26 cards, the same as B, C and F together
items.reasoning: Starting from 10 each and applying the transfers in order: F borrows 2 from A, so A = 8 and F = 12; F gives 5 to C, so F = 7 and C = 15; C gives 3 to B, so C = 12 and B = 13; B gives 6 to D, so B = 7 and D = 16; D passes 1 to E, so D = 15 and E = 11. The final holdings are A = 8, B = 7, C = 12, D = 15, E = 11, F = 7, which sum to 60 as they must. D + E = 26, and of the four options only B + C + F = 7 + 12 + 7 = 26 matches; the others give 27, 22 and 27.

items.value: The water content of the new mixture falls to 25 per cent
items.reasoning: Take the original sample as 30 litres, half water and half milk, so 15 litres of each. One-third of it is 10 litres, containing 5 litres of water and 5 litres of milk. An equal amount of pure milk, 10 litres, is added, giving a 20-litre mixture that still holds only the same 5 litres of water. The water proportion is 5 / 20 = 25 per cent.

items.value: 36 rectangles, squares included
items.reasoning: Every rectangle on such a grid is fixed by choosing two of the horizontal lines for its top and bottom and two of the vertical lines for its left and right sides. That gives 4C2 x 4C2 = 6 x 6 = 36 rectangles. Squares are a special case of rectangles and are already inside this count - with equally spaced lines they number 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 - so the total asked for is 36, not 36 plus a separate square count.

items.value: The express train overtakes the freight train 240 km from Delhi
items.reasoning: In the two hours before the express starts, the freight train covers 2 x 40 = 80 km, so the express begins 80 km behind. The express closes the gap at 60 - 40 = 20 km/hr, so it needs 80 / 20 = 4 hours to catch up, by which time it has travelled 60 x 4 = 240 km from Delhi. The check is that the freight train has then been running 6 hours at 40 km/hr, which is also 240 km.

items.value: The data are inadequate; the highest scorer could be either Neha or Sonal
items.reasoning: Neha is above Randhir, and Sonal is above Shankar, but nothing in the four statements compares Neha with Sonal, so the top place is not fixed. Two sets of marks satisfy every condition and give different winners. With Kunal 40, Debu 10, Randhir 60, Shankar 30, Sonal 35, Neha 61 all four conditions hold and Neha is highest; with Kunal 10, Debu 5, Randhir 60, Shankar 55, Sonal 100, Neha 61 they hold again and Sonal is highest. Since Shankar is bounded only from below by the condition that Kunal and Shankar together exceed Randhir, Sonal can be made arbitrarily large, so no determinate answer exists.
